slides.heading: What the rope locker has in it
body: Three new letters, all from a place you have already walked.
Your first tone rule, and every later one is measured against it.
No new vowel. Everything today runs on the one you have.

slides.heading: All three of them live in one place
body: All three are low class, which puts all three in the harbour.
You have walked it already: the pier, the beach, the doorways.
Learn a district once and every letter living there comes cheaper.

slides.heading: The sound English keeps for the ends of words
body: The name: the sound first, then an everyday word starting with it.
The word means *snake*.
You already make it. Say *sing* and stop on the end. Thai lets it lead.

slides.heading: The rope-maker's daughter
body: She worked the rope locker out where the pier runs to sea.
The snake lived in the coils and kept the rats off the nets.
It is why last lesson's mouse lived at the *other* end of the quay.

slides.heading: The sound the harbour makes
body: At high tide the ropes hum, long and low across the water.
The snake lifts its head from the coil and holds the note with them.

slides.heading: What the pier still keeps
body: The carving where the pier runs out: a coil of rope, and a snake's head rising off it.
The hum at high tide still carries the snake's name.

slides.heading: Put the carving on paper
body: A curve with a head lifting off it: the carving, in one stroke.
Start at the head, high on the left. The pen never lifts.
Write it six or seven times, saying both halves of its name.

slides.heading: Something very large past the wall
body: The sound glides, like the y in *yes*.
The word means *giant* — the wading kind, out of the old stories.

slides.heading: The one who brought the boats home
body: Too big for a boat, so he waded.
He carried the fishing boats home through the storms, two at a time.
He never spoke.

slides.heading: The only sound he made
body: One sound only — a long yawn, rolling in across the water.
It meant the storm was over and the boats were coming home.

slides.heading: Two humps in the sea wall
body: Two humps in the sea wall: his chin and his belly.
No other letter has that pair.

slides.heading: The giant, lying down on your page
body: The chin, then the belly: two bumps on one flank.
No other letter carries that pair.
Head high on the left, down, both bumps, then up.
Write it while saying its name.

slides.heading: A plain silver band
body: The lips round, as for an English *w*.
The word means a *ring* — a silver band on a finger.

slides.heading: The day before he sailed
body: A plain silver band, given the day before he sailed.
The boat came back without him.

slides.heading: Forty years on the steps
body: Forty years, watching the harbour mouth.
Turning it round and round on her finger.

slides.heading: What the fish gave back
body: It had slipped from her finger into the water.
A week later a boy found it inside a fish.

slides.heading: Back on its nail
body: One stroke closing into a single ring, and nothing else on it.
The harbour's word for a circle came from hers.

slides.heading: One closed circle, and then a rule
body: One stroke, closing round into a single circle.
Start at the head, high on the left, and come back to it.
All three on the page now, each one named as you wrote it.

slides.heading: The five that keep going
body: The horse, the mouse, the snake, the giant, the ring.
Every one is a sound you can hold, which is why a syllable may end on it.

slides.heading: Where a flat tone lives
body: The fisherman stands alive in a flat paddy, and nothing has happened to him.
A harbour voice that nothing stops comes out flat.
Flat tones live in the rice paddy.
The other man is from a district you meet next lesson.

slides.prompt: A word begins with the giant's letter, and its long vowel is left open with nothing after it. Which tone does it take, and which rule told you so?

answers: Mid tone, flat from start to finish.
The giant is low class and the syllable is live, so the low class live rule decides it.

slides.heading: You read these, I will keep quiet
body: Read each one before the voice does.
Nothing here needs a letter you have yet to meet.

slides.heading: Read this one
body: A hum, a long vowel, a hum to close it.

slides.heading: And this one
body: The ring, then the snake's letter closing it.

slides.heading: Two lessons in
body: Five letters and one vowel gave you both words.
An address for every letter, and a reason for its tone.
Next: the air stops, at a market with somebody asleep in it.
